claims.text: The as-cast Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Ni alloy has a homogeneous single-phase solid-solution structure.
Cyclic loading at 200–300°C induces a localized martensitic transformation in the alloy.
Stress-induced martensitic transformation preferentially occurs in high-strain or high-local-stress regions.
The transformation converts the ductile single-phase structure into a martensitic phase.
The resulting martensitic phase is harder than the initial single-phase structure.
The resulting martensitic phase is more brittle than the initial single-phase structure.
Localized brittle martensitic zones reduce the alloy's overall fracture toughness.
Localized martensitic zones cause earlier fatigue-crack initiation.
Fatigued specimens will contain martensitic zones detectable by XRD, TEM, or EBSD.
The detectable martensitic zones will correlate with lower global fracture toughness relative to the as-cast control.
The detectable martensitic zones will correlate with earlier fatigue-crack initiation relative to the as-cast control.
The proposed behavior applies to high-cycle fatigue at 200–300°C.
The proposed behavior may not apply at very high or very low temperatures, at substantially different strain rates, or in different alloy compositions.
Transformation-induced phenomena are known to occur in metastable alloys.
Absence of measurable phase transformation under the stated loading conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
The hypothesis would be falsified if cyclic loading produces neither detectable martensitic transformation nor a significant change in toughness or fatigue-crack behavior.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field says absence of measurable transformation alone falsifies the hypothesis, whereas the formal falsification rule requires both absence of transformation and no significant change in toughness or fatigue-crack behavior. These criteria disagree if toughness degrades without detectable martensite.
